title: Over-the-Counter Hearing Aids: What Changed and How to Choose
subtitle: Since 2022 you can buy FDA-regulated hearing aids without a prescription; here is who they suit and what to check before you buy.
excerpt: Hearing aids no longer require a prescription for adults with mild to moderate hearing loss. Here is what the FDA rule changed, how OTC aids differ from cheap amplifiers, and what to look for.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Maybe the TV volume keeps creeping up, or dinner at a busy restaurant has become more nodding than talking. Hearing changes tend to sneak up on us, and for years the only route to a hearing aid ran through a hearing exam and a professional fitting.
That changed in 2022. Today adults can buy a hearing aid in a store or online, the same way you buy reading glasses. Here is what that means for you, and how to choose wisely.

The FDA finalized a rule in August 2022 creating a new category of over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids, and it took effect on October 17, 2022. Adults can now buy these devices directly, without a hearing exam, a prescription or a professional fitting. OTC hearing aids are still regulated by the FDA as medical devices, and their packaging must carry warnings, contact information and the maker's return policy.
Who OTC hearing aids are for

According to the FDA and the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), OTC hearing aids are meant for adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss. "Perceived" means you notice it yourself, even if you have never had a hearing exam.

They are not designed for severe or profound loss. The NIDCD notes that if you have trouble hearing in quiet settings or with loud sounds, OTC aids may not be strong enough. A hearing test with an audiologist is the way to know your actual level of loss.
OTC aids vs. amplifiers vs. prescription aids

items: Prescription hearing aids are fitted and adjusted by a hearing professional, such as an audiologist. People with more severe loss may need one.
OTC hearing aids are self-fitted, usually with a smartphone app or simple controls, for perceived mild to moderate loss.

Personal sound amplification products (PSAPs) are not hearing aids. The FDA says they are for people with normal hearing who want sound boosted in certain situations, like birdwatching, and they are regulated as consumer electronics rather than medical devices.

sections.content: If a cheap device online calls itself a "hearing amplifier" rather than an OTC hearing aid, it is probably a PSAP. The FDA advises looking for the words "OTC" and "hearing aid" displayed prominently on the box, and being wary of "FDA registered" or "FDA certified" claims, which can be misleading.
What to look for before you buy

items: A generous return window. The FDA does not require a warranty, but the box must state the return policy. Look for enough time to try the aids at home, at a restaurant and on the phone.
Batteries: rechargeable or disposable, and how many hours a charge lasts.
Whether you need a smartphone. Many models are set up and adjusted through an app; check that it works with your phone.
Professional help if you want it. Some brands include remote sessions with an audiologist who can fine-tune your settings.
A company that will be around. Lexie, a well-known OTC brand, announced in 2026 that it is winding down U.S. operations, and its app and customer support have ended. Ongoing support matters.

sections.content: These models span a wide price range. Prices are from each maker's own website in October 2026 and change often.

sections.label: Good to Know
sections.content: See a doctor, preferably an ear, nose and throat specialist, before buying OTC if you have ear pain, fluid, pus or blood from the ear in the past six months, sudden or quickly worsening hearing loss, dizziness with hearing loss, or hearing loss or ringing in only one ear. The FDA and NIDCD both list these as warning signs.

OTC hearing aids have made the first step much easier. Start with a hearing test if you can, buy from a company with a solid return policy, and give yourself time to get used to hearing the world again. If OTC isn't enough, an audiologist can take it from there.

products.name: AirPods Pro 3 (with the Hearing Aid feature)
products.blurb: Apple says its Hearing Aid feature has received FDA authorization for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss, and a built-in five-minute hearing test sets it up. Requires a compatible iPhone or iPad, so it best suits people already comfortable with Apple devices.

products.name: All-Day Clear
products.price: About $899.95 (list price; $699.95 on sale at Sennheiser, October 2026)
products.blurb: A self-fitting OTC hearing aid you set up at home through the All-Day Clear app, with a 90-day trial and one-year warranty, according to Sennheiser.

products.name: Enhance Select M1
products.blurb: A rechargeable OTC hearing aid that includes three years of remote care from a licensed audiology team, a 100-day trial when bought from Jabra Enhance, and a three-year warranty that covers loss and damage. Suits people who want professional help without office visits.
